Onboarding.joinStep1: They open the project, then its settings.

Onboarding.joinOutroInbox: The invitation will be waiting in your inbox.

Onboarding.ticketsDropHint: You can also drop a CSV anywhere on this card.
Onboarding.ticketsDropOverlay: Drop your CSV to import it
Onboarding.importDesc: Coming with a backlog? minddy reads CSV exports from Linear, Jira, Notion, Trello and GitHub; and Numo matches the columns for you. Optional. You can do it later from the project settings.
Onboarding.importGuide_linear_1: In Linear, open the view holding your issues.
Onboarding.importGuide_jira_1: In Jira, open your project's List view (or a search).
Onboarding.importGuide_github_1: GitHub has no CSV export: the command below writes one.
Onboarding.importGuide_github_2: Run it inside the repository, with the gh CLI signed in.
Onboarding.importGuide_trello_1: In Trello, open the board menu.
Onboarding.importGuide_trello_2: Print, Export, and Share → Export as CSV (Premium Workspaces only).
Onboarding.importOpenSettings: Do this later from the project settings
Onboarding.importNoProject: Importing writes into a project you own; you don't have one yet. Create a project to import your issues.
Onboarding.mcpDesc: Your coding agent reads your issues, writes its plan and keeps it up to date as it works. Pick yours; or skip, and connect it later from your settings.
Onboarding.keyDesc: The Numo agent can run on your own key; Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter or any compatible endpoint. Its runs are uncapped and your provider bills them. The key goes on or comes off whenever you want.
Onboarding.cyclesDesc: A cycle gathers what you're working on right now, across all projects, over one or two weeks.
Onboarding.finalHint: Something on your mind? “Share feedback”, at the bottom of the sidebar, comes straight to us.
Onboarding.importGuide_notion_1: In Notion, open the database as a full page.
Onboarding.importGuide_notion_2: ⋯ menu, top right → Export → Format: Markdown & CSV.
Onboarding.importGuide_notion_3: Unzip it, then drop the .csv file below.

Onboarding.importGuide_minddy_2: Pick the project and the statuses to include.

Nav.syncPromptText:
Synchronize the local git repo with `origin` so they are strictly identical (0 commits ahead, 0 behind on the current branch).

1. Run `git fetch --all --prune`, then compare the local branch to its upstream.
2. If they have diverged, rebase my local commits on top of the upstream (linear history, no merge commit).
3. Review the resulting history before pushing, then push as a fast-forward. Only use `--force-with-lease` if strictly necessary, and warn me first.
4. Finish by confirming the state: 0 ahead / 0 behind.

Don't touch my uncommitted files; if a rebase conflict occurs, stop and show me the conflict.

launchPrompt.head: Work on {identifier}.
launchPrompt.planExists: This issue already has an implementation plan. Follow it step by step, updating each task's checkbox as you go, then implement the change and verify your work.
launchPrompt.planExistsXl: This issue already has an implementation plan, and it's a large task (XL). Review the plan and refine it if needed, then STOP and ask whether to start implementing now; don't begin coding until I confirm.
launchPrompt.xs: This is a small, well-scoped change (XS). Implement it directly; no need to write a plan first. Verify your work when done.
launchPrompt.s: This is a small task (S). Sketch a short, lightweight plan first only if the change benefits from one, then implement it and verify your work.
launchPrompt.xl: This is a large task (XL). Start by writing a thorough implementation plan on the issue; a short context (goal, approach), ordered checkbox tasks naming the exact files/functions to touch, and a verification step. Then STOP and ask whether to start implementing now; don't begin coding until I confirm.
launchPrompt.default: Start by writing a clear implementation plan on the issue; a short context (goal, approach), ordered checkbox tasks naming the exact files/functions to touch, and a verification step. Once the plan is in place, implement it and verify your work.
launchPrompt.writePlan: Your only job here is to write this issue's implementation plan. Explore the code, then write a short context (goal, approach), ordered checkbox tasks naming the exact files and functions to touch, and a verification step. Grep whatever you're removing or renaming and name every call site: a plan that forgets one reads exactly like a complete one. Save the plan on the issue, then STOP: don't implement anything until I ask.
launchPrompt.reviewPlan: This issue already has an implementation plan: your only job here is to REVIEW it; not to write a new one, and not to implement it. Read it, then go through it task by task against the real code; is each one still accurate (right files, right approach), still needed, and in the right order? Is a step missing? Correct what has drifted, drop what the code no longer calls for, add what's missing, and leave completed tasks and their progress alone. Save the corrected plan on the issue, then STOP and tell me what you changed.
launchPrompt.verifyImplementation: The work on this issue has already been done, at least in part: your only job here is to VERIFY that implementation, not to write a new one. Start with what was asked; the issue, its plan and its comments, where any departure from the plan was argued; then compare them against the real code: is every task marked done really done, and done the way it was specified? Call out the gaps, and tell me which of the two is right (the code is sometimes the better answer, the plan isn't sacred). Then hunt for bugs: broken edge cases, wrong or missing states, call sites the change forgot to update, something the plan asked for that was silently skipped. Fix the ones you can prove by reading the code, and check every fix (the repo's tests, typecheck and lint); what you merely suspect, report it instead of “fixing” it; a speculative change to working code costs more than the bug you imagined. Don't refactor what works, stay inside the issue's scope, and finish by telling me what you verified, what you fixed and what you left alone.
launchPrompt.chainVerifyPlan: This issue already has an implementation plan: your only job here is to REVIEW it; not to write a new one, and not to implement it. Read it, then go through it task by task against the real code; is each one still accurate (right files, right approach), still needed, and in the right order? Is a step missing? Correct what has drifted, drop what the code no longer calls for, add what's missing, and leave completed tasks and their progress alone. Save the corrected plan on the issue, then STOP and tell me what you changed. Then call report_verdict EXACTLY ONCE, as the last thing you do: `ok` true when the plan is sound and ready to be implemented as it stands, false when it is not; and in that case put in `blockers` what has to change first. An automated chain reads that verdict to decide what happens next; without it, nothing moves.
launchPrompt.chainVerifyImplementation: The work on this issue has already been done, at least in part: your only job here is to VERIFY that implementation, not to write a new one. Start with what was asked; the issue, its plan and its comments, where any departure from the plan was argued; then compare them against the real code: is every task marked done really done, and done the way it was specified? Call out the gaps, and tell me which of the two is right (the code is sometimes the better answer, the plan isn't sacred). Then hunt for bugs: broken edge cases, wrong or missing states, call sites the change forgot to update, something the plan asked for that was silently skipped. Fix the ones you can prove by reading the code, and check every fix (the repo's tests, typecheck and lint); what you merely suspect, report it instead of “fixing” it; a speculative change to working code costs more than the bug you imagined. Don't refactor what works, stay inside the issue's scope, and finish by telling me what you verified, what you fixed and what you left alone. Then call report_verdict EXACTLY ONCE, as the last thing you do: `ok` true when the work matches what was asked and you found nothing that must be fixed, false when it does not; and in that case put in `blockers` what has to change. An automated chain reads that verdict: false sends the work back for one more pass with your summary as its instruction, so be precise and be honest.

assistant_model.label: Numo model
assistant_model.desc: Numo in chat and in comment replies.

assistant_reasoning_level.label: Reasoning level
assistant_reasoning_level.desc: Higher levels can improve complex work, but take longer and use more tokens. Applies to Numo chat and comments.

fallback_model.label: Fallback model
fallback_model.desc: Used when the Numo model is left empty.

agent_model.label: Numo agent model
agent_model.desc: Applies to everyone by default. Each user can set their own, and pick another when starting a session.

automation_agent_model.label: Chains and routines model
automation_agent_model.desc: Numo model used by runs launched from an automation.

agent_subagent_favorites.label: Sub-agent favorite models
agent_subagent_favorites.desc: What the agent reads to pick what to run a sub-agent on. It may use any model in the catalogue; these are the ones we recommend. The use case goes into its prompt verbatim: write it in English, for a model that picks.

recommended_models.label: Recommended models
recommended_models.desc: The short list the model picker opens on, everywhere in the app, before anyone types. It hides nothing: searching still reaches the whole catalogue, and a last line opens up more. Order is computed from price, cheapest first, so you only pick WHICH models to recommend. A model above the Pro plan cap (×40) is launchable by nobody.

smart_assign_model.label: Smart assignment
smart_assign_model.desc: Assigns an issue that leaves triage with nobody on it.

smart_fill_enabled.label: Smart-fill
smart_fill_enabled.desc: Lets the create-issue form fill priority, effort, categories and objective on its own. Off here, the toggle disappears from every account.

smart_fill_model.label: Smart-fill model
smart_fill_model.desc: Reads a new issue's title and description and fills its fields. Someone is waiting on it: pick a fast model.

conversation_title_model.label: Conversation titles
conversation_title_model.desc: Names a Numo conversation in a few words, from its first message. A small model is enough.

web_search_enabled.label: Web search
web_search_enabled.desc: Gives Numo and the agents a web search tool (OpenRouter plugin). Each search costs about $0.005, counted against the usage of whoever triggers it.

web_search_model.label: Web search model
web_search_model.desc: Reads the search results and writes the answer. A small model is enough.

dictate_model.label: Dictation → draft
dictate_model.desc: Turns the voice transcript into an issue, objective or task draft.

demo_dictation_enabled.label: Landing page voice demo
demo_dictation_enabled.desc: Lets a visitor with no account try dictation on the home page, on a fictional issue. The only AI call minddy gives away: about $0.0003 a go, capped at ten per IP per hour and 500 a day. Off, the demo says it is unavailable.

feedback_classify_enabled.label: Automatic classification
feedback_classify_enabled.desc: Sorts incoming feedback into categories, drops spam, hides sensitive content and publishes the rest to the board. Without it, every post waits for manual review.

feedback_voice_enabled.label: Dictated feedback
feedback_voice_enabled.desc: Opens the mic in both feedback composers; the public board and internal capture. The take is transcribed, then Numo writes it into the title and body; the spend goes to whoever speaks, or to the board owner for a visitor. Turned off, the mic disappears and typing stays.

feedback_analysis_model.label: Feedback analysis
feedback_analysis_model.desc: Merges obvious duplicates on the board and suggests merges for the rest.

pr_review_model.label: Numo's PR review
pr_review_model.desc: Reads a pull request's diff on demand, then posts a summary and up to five line comments. Keep it different from the agent model: reviewing code with the model that just wrote it only yields the same opinion twice.

import_map_enabled.label: CSV import mapping
import_map_enabled.desc: Lets Numo match the columns of an imported CSV onto minddy's fields. One call per file dropped, on a summary of the columns; never on the rows. Off, the import falls back to matching header names.

import_map_model.label: CSV import mapping model
import_map_model.desc: Reads the column headers, their distinct values and a few samples, and proposes where each column goes. The user sees the proposal and can correct it before importing.

brief_enabled.label: Brief breakdown
brief_enabled.desc: Lets a pasted brief become a proposal of objectives and issues when a project starts. One call per brief, never per issue. Off, a new project starts from an import or from issues typed by hand.

brief_model.label: Brief breakdown model
brief_model.desc: Reads the brief and returns the whole batch at once: 3 to 6 objectives, 10 to 40 issues with their priority and effort. The user reviews the proposal on screen before anything is written.

Delivery goes through the push service of your browser's vendor (Google, Apple or Mozilla depending on the device), which sees that address but not the content — the payload is encrypted end to end and can only be read by the device that subscribed

Privacy.dataGitDesc: access tokens for your GitHub or GitLab repositories are encrypted (AES-256-GCM) before storage. We only reach the repository when you trigger an action that requires it
Privacy.dataKeysDesc: if you provide your own OpenRouter key, it is encrypted (AES-256-GCM) before storage and decrypted only to run your own requests
Privacy.dataBillingDesc: handled by Stripe; we do not store your banking details, only the customer id and the subscription status

Privacy.legalBasisObligationDesc: retention of accounting and invoicing records
Privacy.retentionAccountDesc: kept until your account is deleted
Privacy.retentionContentDesc: kept until you delete it or until your account is closed
Privacy.retentionAgentDesc: the thread of a run (messages exchanged with the model, tool calls and excerpts of their output) is kept 30 days after the run ends, then deleted; afterwards only the metadata (branch, pull request, status) stays attached to the issue. The same 30 days apply to a run played on your own computer
Privacy.retentionFeedbackDesc: kept as long as the project that owns the board exists, and deleted with it. An identity that never posted anything; address verified, then nothing; is deleted after 90 days. Feedback set aside as junk is deleted after 30 days. You can ask the board's publisher to erase your identity at any time: the address and name go, the contributions stay online under a pseudonym
Privacy.retentionBillingDesc: as required by law (10 years for accounting records)
Privacy.transfersText: Your data is hosted within the European Union (Supabase EU region, Ireland). The application is hosted by Vercel (a company based in the United States); any transfers to third countries are covered by appropriate safeguards (Standard Contractual Clauses). Data processing agreements (DPAs) are in place with our sub-processors.
Privacy.transfersProcessors: Sub-processors involved: <supabase>Supabase</supabase> (database, storage, authentication), <vercel>Vercel</vercel> (application hosting, agent execution environments, custom domains), <stripe>Stripe</stripe> (payment), <openrouter>OpenRouter</openrouter> (AI processing), <posthog>PostHog</posthog> (technical usage measurement and persistent analytics with consent), <resend>Resend</resend> (transactional email).
Privacy.transfersAuth: If you choose to sign in with Google or GitHub, those services handle your authentication as independent controllers, under their own policies. If you link a GitHub or GitLab repository, access to that repository happens at your initiative and under your responsibility.
Privacy.processorTitle: Feedback boards: minddy as a processor
Privacy.processorP1: When you open a public feedback board, you become the controller for the data of the people who take part in it, and minddy acts as a processor: we process that data only to provide you with the board, on your instructions.
Privacy.processorP2: Categories involved: verified email address, votes, published feedback and comments, and the audio of a dictated post. minddy uses them for no commercial purpose and trains no model on them. You can ask the board's publisher to erase them; minddy gives them a tool for exactly that; and they are in any case deleted along with the project that owns the board.
Privacy.processorP3: These contributions are processed by AI models before publication: every post is screened to set junk aside and flag what should not be made public, sorted by topic, matched against neighbouring posts, and translated into the team's language when it differs; a dictation adds the transcription of the audio. These steps go through the same providers as the rest of the service; see “AI model providers” below, whose caveat about retention applies here too. Neither the participant's email address nor their name is sent to them: only the text they wrote, or the sound of their voice.
Privacy.agentText: When you trigger the coding agent, the linked repository is cloned into an isolated, ephemeral virtual machine provided by Vercel (Sandbox), destroyed at the end of the run. The code needed for the task is sent to the model through OpenRouter. minddy keeps no copy of the repository beyond the run. From the desktop app you can have a conversation run on your own computer instead, in a folder you attach to the project: the agent then works under your own account, in that folder only. What it does there — its commands, the files it touches, excerpts of what it reads — is recorded in the conversation thread, for the period given above. What it reads outside that folder is not sent to us, and the full output of its tools never leaves your machine.
Privacy.aiProvidersGateway: OpenRouter is not the final recipient of your content: it is a gateway. Each request is routed to the provider of the model in use; DeepSeek, Anthropic, OpenAI or Google depending on the model; which processes it on its own servers, in the United States.
Privacy.aiProvidersRetention: Retention policies differ from one provider to the next: some keep nothing, some log requests for a limited time, some may use them to improve their models. This step is outside our control and we cannot give you any guarantee about it.
Privacy.aiProvidersChoice: Which model is used depends on your choice: the one you pick when launching the agent, or your account's default model. If you configure your own key, the request goes to your provider, under the contract you have with them.
Privacy.thirdPartyText: When you authorize a third-party application (an AI assistant over MCP, for example), it receives an access token and can read and modify your account's data within the permissions granted. The list of these applications, and the ability to revoke them, lives in your account settings.

Privacy.analyticsIntro: minddy measures how the service is used with PostHog, hosted in the European Union. What we collect depends on your choice on the cookie banner, across three states:
Privacy.analyticsAnonymous: Until you answer the banner: measurement is anonymous and cookieless. Nothing is written to your device, neither cookie nor local storage, and the measurement identifier disappears when you close the tab. Two visits therefore cannot be linked to one another. This measurement relies on our legitimate interest in understanding how the service is used; it requires no prior consent because it does not access your device.
Privacy.analyticsAccepted: If you accept: a cookie is set, which lets us link your successive visits and, when you are signed in, attach them to your account so we can understand usage journeys over time.
Privacy.analyticsDeclined: If you decline: the browser stops all PostHog collection, anonymous or account-linked, and no analytics tracker is written to or read from your device. Server-side technical events may still be emitted to measure actions that also exist without a browser, for example through MCP, a webhook or a scheduled job.
Privacy.analyticsMinimization: The browser and server send PostHog only a closed list of technical events that we defined ourselves (for example “an issue was created”, with its status and priority). The content you type never leaves minddy: no issue titles or descriptions, no comments, no messages to the assistant, no file names. Properties are filtered before sending; automatic click capture and on-screen session recording are disabled.

Cookies.title: Cookie policy
Cookies.metaDescription: The cookies minddy sets, what each one is for, and how to change your choice.
Cookies.whatText: A cookie is a small text file stored by your browser when you visit a website. It lets the site remember information about your visit, such as your preferences or your login session.
Cookies.essentialDesc: These cookies are essential for the service to work. They cannot be disabled.
Cookies.essentialCookie3Purpose: Your session on a public feedback board once your email is verified; it is what lets you find your own posts and votes again. Set only on the board you are visiting, including when that board is served from its publisher's own domain
Cookies.analyticDesc: These cookies let us measure usage and improve the service. They are only set with your consent. Before you choose, measurement already happens but without any cookie. See “Cookieless traffic measurement” below.
Cookies.noCookieText: Two measurements run without writing anything to your device. Vercel Analytics measures page traffic with no cookie and no persistent identifier. PostHog runs in that same cookieless mode until you answer the banner: the measurement identifier lives in memory only and disappears when you close the tab, so two visits cannot be linked. No prior consent is required for these, because they do not access your device. If you accept the banner, PostHog then sets the cookie described in the table above; if you decline, it stops all browser collection. Cookieless server-side technical events may continue, as described in the privacy policy.
Cookies.localStorageDesc: Values saved by your browser to remember your preferences and interface state. They never leave your device.
Cookies.localStorageKey1Purpose: Your consent choice for analytics cookies
Cookies.localStorageKey2Purpose: Local cache of your display theme (light, dark or system) — the setting itself lives on your account
Cookies.localStorageKey3Purpose: Drafts of issues and comments not yet submitted
Cookies.localStorageKey4Purpose: The view selected on each board
Cookies.localStorageKey5Purpose: A feedback post being written on a public board
Cookies.thirdPartyText: minddy uses no advertising cookies and no cross-site trackers. No data is shared with advertising networks.
Cookies.preferencesText: On your first visit, a banner lets you accept or decline analytics cookies. You can change that choice at any time:
Cookies.preferencesOption1: Through your browser settings (deleting or blocking cookies)
Cookies.preferencesOption2: By clearing this site's local storage, which brings the banner back
Cookies.preferencesOption3: By writing to <email>hello@minddy.app</email> for any request about your data

Landing.faq_agents_q: Which coding agents can I connect?
Landing.faq_agents_a: Connect an agent that supports MCP, the standard Minddy uses to give AI tools access to project tasks. Minddy provides setup instructions for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code, and Windsurf. You sign in to authorize the connection.
Landing.faq_byok_q: Can I use my own AI provider key?
Landing.faq_byok_a: Yes. Add an API key and choose which AI features use it. Supported calls go to your provider and are billed separately. Calls your key does not cover and cloud code execution still count toward Minddy usage. Compatibility depends on the provider, model, and feature.
Landing.faq_usage_q: How does the included AI usage work?
Landing.faq_usage_a: Each Minddy Cloud plan includes a monthly AI usage allowance. It renews each month, and you can check your usage in your account settings.
Landing.faq_data_a: Your data is not sold or used for advertising. You can export a copy or delete your account from the personal data section in your account settings.
Landing.faq_team_q: Does it work with a team?
Landing.faq_team_a: Yes. Every plan lets you invite people by email. Free includes up to three guests per project; Go and Pro have no guest limit. The project owner does not count toward the limit.
Landing.faq_migrate_q: I'm coming from Linear or Jira: how do I migrate?
Landing.faq_migrate_a: Export your tasks as a CSV file, then import it in your Minddy project settings. Map the columns to task fields such as title, description, status, and priority, and review the import preview.

Pricing.row_members_hint: Invite other people into a project. The owner does not count toward the limit; pending invitations do.
Pricing.row_annual_hint: Pay for a year at the price of ten months. Manage or cancel your subscription from your account.
Pricing.faq_usage_a: AI calls for code agents, the assistant, dictation, feedback and enabled automations use the included budget, along with cloud execution of code agents. Calls made with your own API key are billed by your provider. Managing projects and connecting an external assistant through MCP do not use Minddy's AI budget.
Pricing.faq_overage_q: What happens if I run out of budget?
Pricing.faq_overage_a: Features using the included AI budget pause until it resets the next month, even with yearly billing. You can still manage projects, issues and documents. Minddy does not automatically bill extra usage.
Pricing.faq_change_a: Yes. Open Billing in your account settings to change plans or switch between monthly and yearly billing.
Pricing.faq_refund_a: Yes. Cancel from Billing in your account settings. Your subscription stays active until the end of the paid period, then your account returns to Free.
Pricing.faq_mcp_q: Is the MCP server included in every plan?
Pricing.faq_mcp_a: Yes, including Free. Connect a compatible assistant to read issues, write plans and update tasks. Your assistant's own subscription or API charges may still apply. Numo, Minddy's built-in code agent, is also available on every plan within its AI budget.
Pricing.faq_byok_q: What does my own API key cover?
Pricing.faq_byok_a: You choose which features use your key: code agents, the assistant, automations, dictation or feedback. Compatible AI calls go to your provider and do not use Minddy's included AI budget. Unselected features, calls without a compatible model and cloud execution still use that budget. Your provider's prices and limits apply.

SelfHosting.metaTitle: Self-host the open-source Minddy issue tracker
SelfHosting.metaDescription: Run Minddy's GNU AGPL v3.0 issue tracker and project workspace locally or on your server with the guided self-hosting flow.
SelfHosting.heroTitle: Run Minddy on your own computer or server.
SelfHosting.heroSubtitle: Manage projects and issues on infrastructure you control. This guide starts with the desktop app, then walks you through a personal installation or a shared server for your team.
SelfHosting.promiseBody: Install the open-source version of Minddy where you choose. You manage user accounts, updates and backups.
SelfHosting.promiseOne: Create and manage your own user accounts
SelfHosting.promiseThree: Maintain and back up your installation
SelfHosting.howBody: Minddy manages your projects and issues. Supabase, its required data service, handles accounts, files and live updates. The desktop app connects you to this installation.
SelfHosting.foundation_app_body: Create projects, assign issues and follow your team’s progress.
SelfHosting.foundation_supabase_body: It provides sign-in, the database, file storage and live updates between users.
SelfHosting.foundation_data_title: You choose where data is stored
SelfHosting.foundation_data_body: Host Supabase yourself or use a Supabase Cloud project for your accounts, project data and attachments.
SelfHosting.howBoundary: PostgreSQL alone is not supported. minddy also needs Supabase Auth, Storage, and Realtime.
SelfHosting.routesBody: Choose a personal installation on this computer or a server that several people can access. Both use the desktop app.
SelfHosting.localBody: Keep a personal Minddy installation on this computer. The desktop app starts and stops it; no domain name or remote server is needed.
SelfHosting.teamBody: Give your team access to the same Minddy installation on a dedicated server. Keep it on your private network or add a domain and HTTPS for remote access.
SelfHosting.limitsBody: Manage projects, issues and accounts, export your data and connect AI assistants through MCP. Choose which AI, email, Git and notification services to configure.
SelfHosting.limitsExcluded: Minddy Cloud billing and product analytics are not required. GitHub and GitLab connections can use Minddy’s connection service by default; disable it with --no-forge-relay if you want to manage those connections yourself.
SelfHosting.migrationBody: Export your Cloud data to a JSON transfer file, then import it into your own installation. The transfer includes projects, issues, comments and attachments.

SelfHosting.migrationImportBody: Open Settings → Data → “Import a transfer file”. Existing data is kept. If an imported item’s identifier is already in use, Minddy assigns a new one and lists it in the report.

SelfHostingInstall.privateSupabaseFullNotice: minddy and the complete Supabase stack run on this server. The Supabase API uses the server's private IP on port 8000; keep it available to your LAN only.

SelfHostingInstall.featuresBody: The server includes Numo, Minddy’s coding assistant, and routines for scheduled work. Connect GitHub or GitLab from the app when needed. Choose whether to add email delivery and browser notifications below.

SelfHostingInstall.localPromptTemplate:
You are the installation agent for a supported single-user local minddy instance. Work on this computer and finish with sign-up visible in the desktop app.

Target
- Official guide: MINDDY_GUIDE_URL#local
- Repository: MINDDY_REPOSITORY_URL
- Exact release: MINDDY_RELEASE_TAG
- pnpm: MINDDY_PNPM_VERSION
- Default local origin: MINDDY_LOCAL_ORIGIN
- Desktop app: MINDDY_DOWNLOAD_URL

Safety and scope
- Detect the operating system and CPU architecture before choosing installers. Support macOS, Windows, and Linux.
- Use only official Node.js, Docker, Git, Supabase, and minddy sources. Do not use a moving minddy branch.
- Explain and request approval before any administrator command, package-manager change, reboot, or Docker Desktop installation.
- Never print, paste into chat, or commit generated secrets. Never replace an existing minddy directory or environment file without explicit approval.
- Keep the app bound to loopback. Never expose its ports to the LAN or internet.

Do the work
1. Before any self-host setup, confirm that the signed minddy desktop app is installed from MINDDY_DOWNLOAD_URL and opens. Windows installation must use Microsoft Store; do not look for or download an .exe. Stop here until the app is ready.
2. Inspect what is already installed. Require Node.js 24, Git, Docker with a running daemon, Docker Compose, and the Supabase CLI. Install only missing or incompatible prerequisites using the official instructions for this OS. On Windows, use Docker Desktop and a native terminal; on Linux, install Docker Engine and Compose from Docker's repository; on macOS, use Docker Desktop. Install the Supabase CLI from https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/cli/getting-started and do not install it globally through npm.
3. Verify node --version, git --version, docker --version, docker compose version, docker info, and supabase --version. Resolve failures before continuing.
4. Clone the exact MINDDY_RELEASE_TAG release from MINDDY_REPOSITORY_URL into a new minddy folder, enter it, enable Corepack, activate pnpm MINDDY_PNPM_VERSION, and run pnpm install --frozen-lockfile. If the folder already exists, inspect it and ask before changing it.
5. Open minddy. On Windows or Linux, press Alt to reveal the menu bar. Choose minddy > Connect to a Server… > Run local minddy on this computer and select the cloned folder. Do not start pnpm self-host:local in a separate terminal: the desktop app must own startup and shutdown.
6. Wait until the desktop app starts the local backend, verifies health, and displays sign-up. Do not create the user's account.
7. Report the final origin, selected folder, and desktop-owned startup behavior. Verify that quitting minddy stops both services and reopening it starts the saved folder again. Finish only when sign-up is visible in the desktop app. If blocked, state the exact failed command, its useful output, and the next concrete action instead of guessing.
SelfHostingInstall.localAutostartPrompt: Final startup behavior: use the desktop app on macOS, Windows, or Linux as the only startup owner. Verify that quitting minddy stops both minddy and its local Supabase backend and that reopening the app starts the saved folder again. Do not leave the user with a terminal-owned server or a second startup command.
SelfHostingInstall.teamPromptTemplate:
You are installing a supported shared minddy instance. Work through the entire setup and finish with sign-up visible in the desktop app.

Chosen setup
- Guide: MINDDY_GUIDE_URL#team
- Repository: MINDDY_REPOSITORY_URL
- Exact release: MINDDY_RELEASE_TAG
- pnpm: MINDDY_PNPM_VERSION
- Access: MINDDY_ACCESS_MODE
- minddy address: MINDDY_APP_ORIGIN
- Administrator email: MINDDY_ADMIN_EMAIL
- Backend: MINDDY_SUPABASE_MODE
- Desktop app: MINDDY_DOWNLOAD_URL

Safety
- Use the dedicated Linux server selected by the user. Inspect its distribution, CPU architecture, memory, disk, network, and existing files before changing anything.
- Use official sources and the exact minddy release. Never use a moving branch.
- Ask before administrator commands, firewall changes, package installation, or replacing a file. Preserve SSH access.
- Never print, expose, or commit passwords, database URLs, private keys, service-role keys, or generated secrets.

Do the work
1. Before changing the server, confirm that the signed minddy desktop app is installed from MINDDY_DOWNLOAD_URL on the user's macOS, Windows, or Linux computer and opens. Windows installation must use Microsoft Store; do not look for or download an .exe. Stop here until the app is ready.
2. Apply this network rule exactly: MINDDY_NETWORK_SETUP
3. Install only missing prerequisites: Node.js 24, Git, Docker Engine 27 or later, and Docker Compose 2.29 or later. Use their official Linux repositories. Verify node --version, git --version, docker --version, docker compose version, and docker info. Enable Corepack and pnpm MINDDY_PNPM_VERSION.
4. Clone MINDDY_RELEASE_TAG from MINDDY_REPOSITORY_URL into a new folder and run pnpm install --frozen-lockfile. Inspect and ask before changing an existing deployment.
5. Prepare the selected backend: MINDDY_SUPABASE_PREPARATION
6. Run this installer command from the minddy folder, answer any secure credential prompts, and let it finish:
MINDDY_INSTALL_COMMAND
7. Configure account email delivery, inspect every container, then run:
MINDDY_DOCTOR_COMMAND
Resolve every failed check. Verify MINDDY_APP_ORIGIN/api/health, deliver one test account email, and create a first restorable backup away from the server. Do not create the user's account.
8. On the user's computer, open minddy. On Windows or Linux, press Alt to reveal the menu bar. Choose minddy > Connect to a Server…, enter MINDDY_APP_ORIGIN, and confirm that sign-up appears in the desktop app.
9. Report the final address, backend choice, running services, backup location, stop/restart commands, and the exact desktop sign-up step. If blocked, ask one precise question and retain all completed work.

Mcp.flow_track_body: Ask the assistant to mark each plan task as complete when it finishes. Your team can follow progress directly on the issue.
Mcp.flow_track_prompt: Work through the plan on MIN-42 and keep its tasks up to date.
Mcp.flow_create_body: Describe the work you agreed on. The assistant creates issues with a description and priority, ready for your team to review.
Mcp.flow_create_prompt: Create issues in minddy for everything we just decided.
Mcp.faq_free_q: Do I need a paid plan to connect an agent?
Mcp.faq_free_a: No. Connecting an external assistant is included in every Minddy plan, including Free. Any subscription required by your assistant is separate.
Mcp.faq_agents_q: Which agents does it work with?
Mcp.faq_agents_a: Setup instructions are provided for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code and Windsurf. Other assistants need support for remote MCP connections with OAuth sign-in.
Mcp.faq_key_q: Where do I create an API key?
Mcp.faq_key_a: You do not need an API key. Sign in to Minddy in your browser and approve access when you connect. You can revoke that access from your account settings.

Alternatives.compareSubtitle: Compare issue tracking, AI assistance, collaboration costs and hosting options.
Alternatives.minddy_teammate: No additional charge per collaborator; plan limits apply
Alternatives.minddy_agents: Built-in assistant, AI coding agents and connections to compatible assistants via MCP
Alternatives.minddy_pages: Project pages with subpages, version history and sharing
Alternatives.minddy_feedback: Public request boards with voting; turn selected requests into issues
Alternatives.minddy_hosting: Hosted by Minddy, or install the open-source application on your own servers
Alternatives.minddy_setup: Issue statuses ready to use; optional CSV import
Alternatives.minddy_builtFor: One person or a small team
Alternatives.productTitle: What you can do with minddy
Alternatives.productSubtitle: Track bugs and features, document your projects and work with AI coding agents in one place.
Alternatives.feature_openSource_title: Read, change or host the code
Alternatives.feature_openSource_body: The source code is available under AGPL v3. Review it, contribute changes or install the open-source application on your own servers.
Alternatives.feature_pages_body: Write specifications and record decisions in project pages. Organize subpages, view earlier versions and share pages. Numo and connected AI assistants can read and update them.
Alternatives.feature_scratchpad_body: Jot down an idea or a task. Turn it into an issue when you want to track it with your project, or send it to a coding agent.
Alternatives.feature_feedback_body: Publish a board where users submit requests and vote. Merge duplicates and turn selected requests into issues. Each linked request shows progress as its issue status changes.
Alternatives.feature_pullRequests_body: Open an issue's pull request to read code changes, automated check results and comments. Approve or merge it from minddy.
Alternatives.feature_voice_body: Dictate a bug or feature request and minddy fills in the issue form. You can also edit individual fields by voice.
Alternatives.checkedNote: Checked on {date} against official documentation and pricing.
Alternatives.billingNote: A project's capacity depends on its owner's plan. Inviting a collaborator does not add a per-person charge to that owner's bill. Each collaborator keeps their own account limits and AI allowance.
Alternatives.aiNote: AI models and allowances depend on your plan. With a compatible personal API key, the provider bills AI calls for the functions you configure. Cloud code-agent execution still uses your included budget. Hosting on your own servers may cost extra.
Alternatives.feature_agents_title: Ask AI to work on an issue
Alternatives.feature_agents_body: Ask a coding agent to plan and implement an issue, then review its proposed changes. Run it in the cloud or on your computer through the desktop app. You can also connect your own assistant via MCP.
Alternatives.feature_numo_body: Numo is minddy's built-in AI assistant. Ask it to find an issue, explain a project decision or update a page. You can connect external tools through MCP, a standard for connecting AI assistants to applications.
Alternatives.feature_routines_body: Give AI instructions to run on a project at a set time. For example, ask for a weekly review of open issues. You can also create recurring issues and rules that automate status changes.
Alternatives.feature_planning_body: Group issues by objective, split work into smaller issues and see which tasks depend on others. Save filtered lists and choose work from several projects for your week or fortnight.
Alternatives.feature_capture_body: Write a private note, dictate an issue or find actions with the command menu. Use minddy in your browser or in the macOS, Windows and Linux apps.
Alternatives.migrationTitle: Try minddy with your existing tasks
Alternatives.migrationBody: Export your tasks from {name} as a CSV file, then import them into a minddy project. Check which columns match each issue field. Connect your code repository and AI assistant when you are ready.
Alternatives.verdictSubtitle: Choose the workflow that fits your team.

Changelog.metaDescription: Read Minddy’s latest product updates, with release dates and explanations of what each change lets you do.
Changelog.feedBannerTitle: Follow Minddy updates in your feed reader
Changelog.feedBannerBody: RSS lets you follow updates without an account. Copy this page’s address into an RSS reader to receive new release announcements.
Changelog.entry_open-source_body: The application is licensed under GNU AGPL v3. Its source repository will open in the coming days, with guides to install Minddy on your own computer or server and contribute to it.
Changelog.entry_desktop-app_title: Use Minddy on macOS, Windows and Linux
Changelog.entry_desktop-app_body: Minddy now has its own desktop app on all three platforms, with automatic updates and a server picker for Cloud or self-hosted instances. Download the build made for your system and work outside the browser.
Changelog.entry_activity-breakdowns_title: Take stock of what you have accomplished
Changelog.entry_activity-breakdowns_body: Your personal statistics now give you a clearer view of completed issues, pace and time spent. Breakdowns by project, category and objective help you understand what you have accomplished across all your work.
Changelog.entry_custom-avatar_title: Choose the face you show in Minddy
Changelog.entry_custom-avatar_body: Pick a generated Lorelei avatar or upload your own image from your profile. The same avatar follows you through projects, comments and conversations.
Changelog.entry_feedback-page-tabs_title: Add documentation to your public feedback page
Changelog.entry_feedback-page-tabs_body: Published project pages can now appear as tabs on your public feedback page. Add a roadmap, documentation or community rules for visitors to read alongside suggestions.
Changelog.entry_account-transfer_title: Move your account to another Minddy instance
Changelog.entry_account-transfer_body: Export your account, then import it into another Minddy instance. Projects, issues, pages, settings and personal history come with you; passwords, provider keys and subscriptions stay behind.
Changelog.entry_own-ai-everywhere_title: Use your own AI provider across Minddy
Changelog.entry_own-ai-everywhere_body: One key can now power Numo, Smart-fill, transcription, feedback review and the rest of Minddy’s AI. Compatible local models work too, so supported tasks can stay on your computer.
Changelog.entry_github-dependencies_title: Keep GitHub issue dependencies in sync
Changelog.entry_github-dependencies_body: When a GitHub issue blocks another one, the linked Minddy issues now show the same relationship. Changes made on GitHub continue to update the issue panel automatically.
Changelog.entry_live-page-edits_title: See page edits as they happen
Changelog.entry_live-page-edits_body: When someone else edits a project page, their changes now appear while you have it open. Autosave keeps your own work in step instead of leaving two tabs to overwrite each other.
Changelog.entry_local-agent_title: Run the coding agent on your own computer
Changelog.entry_local-agent_body: The desktop app can attach a project to a local folder and run Numo there. You see file changes as it works, and they stay in your working copy until you decide what to do with them.
Changelog.entry_pages_title: Keep your project's notes and specs in pages
Changelog.entry_pages_body: Create project documents and organize them into pages and subpages in the sidebar. Add text blocks and notebook tasks, then link a page to an issue as a resource. Numo, Minddy’s AI assistant, can read and edit these pages too.
Changelog.entry_smart-fill_title: AI suggests details for your new issues
Changelog.entry_smart-fill_body: Smart-fill uses AI to read an issue’s title and description and fill in its priority, effort, categories and objective. You can turn it off for one issue or for all issues in your account settings.
Changelog.entry_board-multi-select_title: Select several cards on the board and move them together
Changelog.entry_board-multi-select_body: Draw a rectangle across the board to select the cards it covers. Dragging one of them carries the whole selection to another column, in the order you see them.
Changelog.entry_issue-sync_title: Repository issues and minddy issues stay in step
Changelog.entry_issue-sync_body: Issues imported from GitHub or GitLab arrive with their labels, their priority and their assignee, and keep following the remote one. Closing an issue in minddy now closes it on the repository too.
Changelog.entry_invite-by-email_title: Invite someone who doesn't have an account yet
Changelog.entry_invite-by-email_body: Add them by email address, and they get an invitation to join the project. They create their account from that email and land straight in the project. Pending invitations expire on their own.
Changelog.entry_routines_title: Schedule recurring work for your coding agent
Changelog.entry_routines_body: Give the coding agent instructions for a repository and choose a schedule, such as a security review every Monday. Each routine runs automatically, proposes fixes in a pull request and reports its findings. Review past runs in the Routines tab.
Changelog.entry_push-notifications_title: Get a notification when something lands in your inbox
Changelog.entry_push-notifications_body: Notifications turn on device by device, from the device itself. Each one is listed in your account settings, with when it was added and its last notification, and can be switched off or removed. On iPhone, add minddy to your home screen first.
Changelog.entry_project-start_title: Start a project from a brief, and get your first issues
Changelog.entry_project-start_body: Creating a project now asks where you are starting from. Coming from another tool, you drop your CSV export. Starting from nothing, you describe the project in a few lines: Numo asks what is missing, then proposes the issues and objectives, which you review before they exist.
Changelog.entry_smart-assign_title: Issues find their assignee on their own
Changelog.entry_smart-assign_body: Describe in plain words the kind of work each member takes on, and any issue leaving triage without an assignee gets one. It switches on in the project settings. Alone on a project, the issues simply come to you.
Changelog.entry_feedback-comments_title: Your feedback board now takes comments
Changelog.entry_feedback-comments_body: Visitors can now comment on a suggestion and reply to other comments on your public feedback page. They verify their email before their first comment; only an avatar is shown beside it. You can disable comments at any time.
Changelog.entry_resources_title: Attach a link to an issue, not just a file
Changelog.entry_resources_body: Issues and objectives now hold resources: files as before, and web addresses. Drop a file straight onto an issue to attach it. Everything sits in one place, ready to open or download.
Changelog.entry_feedback-setup_title: Add a feedback button to your app with guided setup
Changelog.entry_feedback-setup_body: Choose how to collect suggestions, whether users are already signed in and where the button should appear in your app. The guide prepares instructions for your coding assistant. You can also give them to Numo to implement the change and open a pull request.
Changelog.entry_feedback-translation_title: Feedback written in another language arrives translated
Changelog.entry_feedback-translation_body: Numo, which already reads every submission before it goes live, now translates the ones written in a language other than yours. The original stays one click away. It works on feedback from the board and from your own app alike.
Changelog.entry_export-issues_title: Export your issues as a CSV file
Changelog.entry_export-issues_body: Pick the projects and the statuses to include, and get a file. It follows minddy's own import format, so it can be dropped straight back into another project.
Changelog.entry_pull-requests_title: Review and merge your pull requests without leaving minddy
Changelog.entry_pull-requests_body: Every pull request on a linked repository now opens inside minddy: the changes line by line, the commits, the checks and the whole conversation. You comment, approve, resolve a thread or merge, under your own GitHub or GitLab account.
Changelog.entry_pr-review_title: Ask Numo to review a pull request
Changelog.entry_pr-review_body: Numo reads the changes, the issue and the discussion, then posts a summary and its comments on the lines concerned. You reply to them like any other review. And when you are the one requesting changes, Numo can go back and make them.
Changelog.entry_automations_title: Let the agent chain plan, code and checks on its own
Changelog.entry_automations_body: Pick an automation preset, the projects and the efforts it runs on, and an issue reaching To do starts the loop by itself: the plan, the implementation, then a check of the work. On the biggest ones, it waits for your go-ahead before writing any code.
Changelog.entry_recurring-issues_title: Issues that come back on their own
Changelog.entry_recurring-issues_body: An issue can now repeat every day, week, month or year. Close it, and the next one is already waiting in the backlog, at the right date. The project settings list every recurring issue, to change a rhythm or stop one.
Changelog.entry_own-api-key_title: Run the coding agent on your own API key
Changelog.entry_own-api-key_body: Add an Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter or compatible key, at signup or later from your account. The agent's runs are uncapped; your provider bills them on whichever model you want. The key is encrypted and removable in one click.
Changelog.entry_mentions_title: Mention a person, an issue or an objective as you write
Changelog.entry_mentions_body: In a description or a comment, typing an at sign now suggests the people on the project, its issues, its objectives and your projects. What you pick becomes a link others can follow, and anyone you name is notified.
Changelog.entry_trash_title: Deleted issues wait in the trash
Changelog.entry_trash_body: Issues, objectives, feedback and projects you delete land in the trash for 30 days, with who removed them and when. Restore one in a click, or empty the trash yourself.
Changelog.entry_import-issues_title: Bring in the issues you already have
Changelog.entry_import-issues_body: minddy reads a Linear, Jira or Trello CSV export, at signup or later from the project settings. And when a project is linked to a GitHub or GitLab repository, every issue opened there arrives here, its status following the remote one.
Changelog.entry_home-attention_title: The home page shows what needs you now
Changelog.entry_home-attention_body: The home page now lists issues with approaching deadlines, with overdue work first. A second section brings together incoming issues and feedback waiting for review across your projects. Each item shows which project it belongs to.
Changelog.entry_zen-mode_title: Keep the board, hide the rest
Changelog.entry_zen-mode_body: Zen mode puts away the sidebar and the header, leaving your work alone on screen. It turns on from the command palette, and off the same way.
Changelog.entry_account-data_title: Take everything with you, or delete it all
Changelog.entry_account-data_body: The account settings now export a JSON file holding your account, projects, issues, comments and conversations. The same page deletes your account for good, after telling you exactly what goes with it.
Changelog.entry_agent-brief_title: Brief the agent before it starts
Changelog.entry_agent-brief_body: Launching the coding agent on an issue now takes an instruction of your own, on top of what the issue already says. You also pick how long it thinks before acting, from a short pass to the deepest reasoning.
Changelog.entry_mcp-page_title: A setup guide for connecting AI assistants
Changelog.entry_mcp-page_body: Connect an AI assistant to read and update your Minddy projects through MCP. The new guide provides the server address, setup instructions for each supported assistant and examples to try. It also includes instructions you can copy to your assistant to help set up the connection.
Changelog.entry_localised-site_title: The public site now speaks French at its own address
Changelog.entry_localised-site_body: Pricing, legal pages and the home page each exist at a French URL of their own, instead of switching language behind one address. The pages also got noticeably lighter, so they open faster on a phone.
Changelog.entry_search-everywhere_title: Search issues and objectives from anywhere
Changelog.entry_search-everywhere_body: The command palette now searches every issue and objective you have access to, across projects, and no longer just the ones on screen. Results come back as you type.
Changelog.entry_notebook-agent_title: Launch an agent from the task notebook
Changelog.entry_notebook-agent_body: Ask the coding agent to work on a task from your personal notebook. You can launch it directly from the task, without creating a project issue first.
Changelog.entry_notifications_title: Notifications you can actually keep up with

Automations.title: Automations
Automations.description: Chain the Numo agent's four steps; plan, review the plan, implement, verify; instead of clicking through them one at a time. What runs depends on the issue's effort.
Automations.presetHint: One preset for all the projects you own. Pick which ones it runs on below.
Automations.presetNoneSelected: No preset; nothing runs, whatever the toggles below say.
Automations.presetLoopByEffortDesc: XS and S go straight to code. On an M, the Numo agent writes a plan, implements it, then checks its own work. L and XL add a review of the plan; and wait for your go-ahead before any code is written.
Automations.presetLoopByEffortShort: Plan, code and checks; sized by effort.
Automations.presetPlanAndVerifyDesc: The Numo agent writes the plan when an issue reaches “To do”, and checks the work when it reaches “In review”. It never writes the code itself; that part stays yours.
Automations.presetPlanAndVerifyShort: Plans before, checks after. You write the code.
Automations.presetPlanOnlyDesc: When an issue reaches “To do”, the Numo agent explores the code and writes its implementation plan on the ticket. It stops there; nothing gets coded.
Automations.presetImplementOnlyDesc: When an issue reaches “To do”, the Numo agent goes straight to the code; no plan written first, no check afterwards. Best kept for small, well-described issues.
Automations.presetImplementOnlyShort: Straight to the code, no plan, no check.
Automations.presetVerifyOnlyDesc: When an issue reaches “In review”, the Numo agent re-reads the work against the plan and the comments, fixes what it can prove, and reports the rest.
Automations.presetVerifyOnlyShort: Re-reads the work when it reaches review.
Automations.projectsHint: Only projects you own. Arming the loop on a production repo isn't the same decision as on a sandbox.
Automations.effortsHint: Turn the loop off on the efforts you'd rather keep by hand. An issue with no effort follows the M row, like everywhere else in minddy.
Automations.modelsHint: A small model on your XS, a strong one on your XL. Empty means your default model, the same one a manual launch uses. The preset still tunes the reasoning level step by step.
Automations.costDesc: Estimated from this project's history, as a share of your plan's monthly budget.
Automations.costFallback: No history yet on this project; these are rough defaults, they'll sharpen as sessions run.
Automations.chainRunning: The Numo agent is on it; step {step}
Automations.delayHint: Room to change your mind. During the delay the loop waits; and it cancels itself if you move the issue elsewhere, for instance by copying its prompt to do the work yourself. Once started, it runs its steps back to back.

Routines.noEligibleProject: A routine runs on a repository, and only the project's owner can schedule one. Link a repository to a project you own to create your first routine.

Routines.stepProjectDesc: The routine opens an isolated agent sandbox and clones this project's repository for every run.
Routines.stepJobDesc: This is the instruction the agent receives, every time. Nobody will be there to clarify it; say what to look at and what to do with what it finds.
Routines.stepModelDesc: Frozen on the routine: the strongest model for a security review, the cheapest for a monthly inventory.
Routines.stepScheduleDesc: The hour is read in the timezone below; check the first run before validating.
Routines.createdDesc: It will run on its own in an isolated server sandbox. Its runs are available here, in the Routines tab.
Routines.executionEnvironment: Runs in an isolated sandbox on the server, without a desktop app.
Routines.promptPlaceholder: Review the code for security flaws, and open a pull request for what you can fix.
Routines.exampleSecurity: Review the repository for security flaws: unvalidated input, secrets in the code, missing authorization checks. Open a pull request for what you can fix with confidence, and report the rest.
Routines.exampleDeps: Check the dependencies for known vulnerabilities and outdated majors. Bump what can be bumped without breaking the build; run the tests; and open a pull request. Report anything that needs a decision.
Routines.exampleTests: Find the code paths that changed recently and are not covered by tests. Write the missing tests for the two or three that matter most, run them, and open a pull request.
Routines.spendCapHelp: A routine runs unattended, so every run stops at a share of your monthly usage; a weekly routine should not take the month. Raise it for one that has to see the job through. It does not apply when you run on your own API key.
Routines.spendCapValueDesc: One run stops at {percent}% of your monthly usage.
Routines.spendCapDefaultDesc: Default. Enough to keep coming back all month without eating your budget.
Routines.spendCapNoneDesc: One run can spend everything you have left this month.
